title: Practice: Design a Risk Management System
summary: A fintech favourite: a transaction risk engine with pluggable rules, scoring and hard blocks, sliding-window velocity checks, hot-reloadable config, audit and manual review, done one step at a time.

steps.title: Clarify the requirements
hints: "Risk management" is ambiguous: payments fraud, trading limits, credit. Ask which one, then commit.
Ask what the engine *returns*. A yes/no? A score? Reasons? Who acts on a "maybe"?
checklist: Domain pinned down (payment transaction risk) and where the engine sits in the flow
Decision outcomes: ALLOW / REVIEW / BLOCK, with reasons
Concrete rule types: amount, velocity, blocklist, device, geography
Rules configurable without a deploy
Latency budget, audit trail, and behaviour when a rule fails

steps.title: Identify entities
hints: Split the nouns into *input* (what's evaluated), *logic* (rules, policy) and *output* (results, decision, audit).
What state does a velocity rule need that the other rules don't?
checklist: Transaction and a context/profile as immutable inputs
Rule interface; RuleResult with score, verdict and reason
A DecisionPolicy separate from the rules
Stateful stores (velocity counters, lists) separate from rule logic
Assessment as the auditable output

steps.title: Draw the class diagram
hints: The engine is the hub. Rules are many small strategies around it.
Where does configuration come from, and who builds the rule objects from it?
checklist: RiskEngine → Rule (many), DecisionPolicy, listeners
Concrete rules implementing one interface
A factory/registry building rules from config
Observers for audit log, review queue and alerts

steps.title: Rule evaluation and the decision
hints: There are two kinds of signal: "this alone is enough to block" and "this adds suspicion". Model both.
What happens if a rule throws or times out? Allow (fail open) or block (fail closed)?
checklist: Each rule returns a score and an optional hard verdict
Total score mapped through thresholds; the decision is max(score-based, hard verdict)
Short-circuit on a hard BLOCK, with cheap rules ordered first
Rule errors handled explicitly (to REVIEW), never silently allowed
Every rule hit kept, with its reason, for audit

steps.title: Velocity checks: sliding windows
hints: "More than 5 transactions in 10 minutes per user." What do you store per user?
Compare a fixed window, a sliding log and sliding buckets for memory and accuracy.
checklist: Sliding-window log (deque of timestamps) with eviction
Trade-off with bucketed counters for high volume
Key design: per user, per card, per device, per IP
Whether to count attempts or only approved transactions

steps.title: Extensibility, config and concurrency
hints: Two payments from the same user arrive at once, and the limit is 5 per 10 minutes with 4 already used. Trace it.
Rules get updated while 1,000 requests are mid-evaluation. What do they see?
checklist: Atomic record-and-count (per-key lock / compute / Redis INCR or Lua)
Immutable config snapshot swapped atomically (copy-on-write)
Composite/Specification for AND/OR rules from config
Decorators for timeouts, metrics and shadow mode

steps.title: Code the core
hints: Start with `Rule`, `RuleResult` and `Decision`, then the engine loop, then two or three concrete rules.
The velocity store needs one method only: `recordAndCount(key, at, window)`.
checklist: Rule interface and three or more concrete rules
Engine combining scores and hard verdicts, with short-circuit
Thread-safe velocity store
Config snapshot that can be swapped at runtime

steps.title: Answer the follow-ups
hints: For each one, decide whether it's a new rule, a new policy, a new listener or a new store.
Think about what an ops or risk analyst needs to do without an engineer.
checklist: Shadow / dry-run mode for a new rule
ML model score as just another rule
Per-merchant thresholds
Scaling across many instances
